newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sees no money laundering in Texas Fed branch.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sees no money laundering in Texas Fed branch.

text.p: Billions of dollars of mysterious cash surpluses building up at a Federal Reserve branch in Texas are not the result of illegal money laundering activity, U.S. government officials told Congress on Thursday.
The San Antonio branch of the Federal Reserve bank of Dallas reported a cash surplus of almost $3 billion in 1995.
Rep Henry Gonzalez, Democrat of Texas, charged in January that the surplus could be the result of money laundering by Mexican drug dealers and called for Congressional hearings.
But a study by the Internal Revenue Service's Criminal Investigation Division turned up no evidence linking the surplus to money laundering.

"We can now say definitively that cash surpluses at the Federal Reserve Banks are not indicators of moeny laundering," Stanley Morris, director of the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network or FinCEN, said in prepared testimony for a Congressional hearing Thursday.
A cash surplus results when commercial banks around a Fed branch deposit more currency than the branch sends back to the Fed.
The San Antonio Branch surplus was mostly the result of currency transfers between U.S. border banks and Mexican banks, the IRS study found.
Tourism in the area and export retail sales to Mexican residents also contributed to the surplus.
